acceptable.choice: Keep Ruby/Rails/Sidekiq and scale processing out across more worker processes and containers
acceptable.why: 50,000 images × 0.15–0.4 s comes to about 2–5.5 CPU-hours, so six hours of wall-clock time means roughly one core was doing the work; about 8–16 cores working in parallel gets the batch under an hour with no rewrite.

acceptable.choice: Autoscale Sidekiq workers on queue depth or latency (for example KEDA, the cloud provider's autoscaler, or a scheduled scale-up), ideally on spot or preemptible instances
acceptable.why: Catalogue uploads come in bursts, so paying for many cores only while a queue exists meets the one-hour target and keeps cost per image low.

acceptable.choice: Run one Sidekiq process per core (or per vCPU pair) with modest thread concurrency, and tune libvips' own threading (VIPS_CONCURRENCY)
acceptable.why: Ruby's global interpreter lock (GVL), and libvips threads competing with Sidekiq threads, can quietly cap a single process at about one core; process-level parallelism avoids that.

acceptable.choice: Optimise the image pipeline inside libvips: decode once, use thumbnail and shrink-on-load, produce all variants from one load, stream from and to object storage, and avoid ImageMagick or ActiveStorage variant overhead
acceptable.why: This cuts CPU per image directly, which helps cost and throughput, and it is a small change in the existing code.

acceptable.choice: Optimise the tagging model: load it once per process rather than per job, use ONNX Runtime, quantise it, feed it a small input resolution, and batch inference
acceptable.why: The model is probably the largest share of the 150–400 ms, and these changes reduce cost per image far more than changing the host language would.

acceptable.choice: If the model is only practical in Python, move just the tagging into a small Python inference worker or sidecar and keep the rest in Ruby
acceptable.why: This is a targeted change made for an ecosystem reason, not a rewrite, and the coding agent can maintain it.

acceptable.choice: Per-customer or per-batch queues, with priority or rate limits, so a 50,000-image upload does not starve other customers
acceptable.why: This becomes an operational need as soon as faster bulk processing is available to more than one pilot customer.

acceptable.choice: Measure a managed vision or tagging API, or burst compute such as Cloud Run jobs, Lambda or Batch, against self-hosted inference
acceptable.why: These are reasonable options for a two-person team if the per-image price beats the cost of running and scaling their own CPUs, which needs measuring.

ruled_out.choice: Rewriting the processing in Go, Rust, C++ or Elixir now
ruled_out.why: The CPU time is spent in libvips (C) and the model, not in Ruby, so a rewrite barely changes per-image CPU or cost; it also costs weeks of a two-person team's time and moves the code into a language the founder can't review.

ruled_out.choice: Rewriting the processing in Python wholesale
ruled_out.why: It is no faster for libvips work and creates a second codebase; only the tagging model might justify Python, and only as a narrow piece.

ruled_out.choice: Just raising Sidekiq thread concurrency in the existing containers
ruled_out.why: It adds no CPU; because of the GVL and libvips' own threads it may give no speed-up and can cause memory blow-ups.

ruled_out.choice: Kubernetes plus Kafka or a microservices re-architecture
ruled_out.why: That is heavy operational overhead for two people when the Sidekiq/Redis queue already provides the fan-out they need.

ruled_out.choice: GPUs bought up front for the whole pipeline
ruled_out.why: libvips work won't use them, and for the model they make sense only if measurement shows inference dominates and batches keep the GPU busy; otherwise they raise cost per image.

ruled_out.choice: Permanently over-provisioning a large fixed fleet
ruled_out.why: It meets the burst target but undermines cost per processed image, which is one of the two things the team cares about.

must_mention: Do the arithmetic: 2–5.5 CPU-hours of work finished in 6 wall-clock hours means the run was effectively serial or close to it, so this is a parallelism and capacity problem, not a language problem.
Ruby is not the hot path: libvips is C, and the model runs in native code. Ruby's per-image overhead is a few milliseconds out of 150–400.
A rewrite would barely change cost per image, because the per-image CPU stays roughly the same in any language.
Profile before changing anything: split time into download, decode, resize and watermark, tagging, upload and queue wait, and check whether the model is reloaded on every job.
Watch for the GVL and libvips thread contention; prefer several processes per container and tune VIPS_CONCURRENCY.
Scale workers elastically on queue depth so the burst is fast and idle time costs little.
The tagging model is the most likely place to make each image cheaper (quantisation, batching, smaller input, load once).
Staying on Ruby keeps the founder able to review the agent's code, which matters for this team.
red_flags: Recommending a rewrite in Go or Rust as the fix, or claiming it would make processing 5–10× faster.
Agreeing that Ruby is the problem without doing the CPU-hours versus wall-clock arithmetic.
Ignoring that the founder reviews the code in Ruby, and that a new language weakens their oversight of agent-written code.
Suggesting only more Sidekiq threads in one process as the fix.
Proposing Kubernetes, Kafka, a service mesh or a microservices split for a two-person team.
Recommending GPUs or a large always-on fleet without considering cost per image.
Giving no measurement or profiling step before making changes.
Ignoring multi-tenant fairness when a single 50,000-image batch is added to the queue.
unknowns: How the 150–400 ms splits between libvips operations and tagging inference.
How the tagging model runs: an in-process Ruby binding (ONNX Runtime gem), a Python service, or an external API, and whether it is loaded once per process or once per job.
The current number of Sidekiq processes, threads per process, cores per container and container count, which shows how much parallelism they actually got.
Whether the libvips and model bindings release the GVL during native calls.
How much time goes to I/O: downloading originals, uploading outputs and storage latency.
Memory per worker process, which limits how many workers fit on each instance and therefore cost.
What autoscaling and spot or preemptible options the cloud provider offers, and how fast instances start.
How often and how large catalogue bursts are, and whether the one-hour target is a contract or an expectation.
Whether the pilot customers would accept a managed tagging API's per-image price and data handling.
